title: States as actions: the "passive" side of Japanese
summary: Many Japanese verbs describe states or changes that English can only say with "is" or a passive. In Japanese the thing itself does the verb.

blocks.text: Japanese has no true passive voice (the receptive れる / られる only receives an action). But Japanese does have a **passive outlook**. The first two verbs, **ある** (be) and **する** (do), come as a pair, and Japanese tends to put being before doing, while English is more activist. As a result many Japanese verbs depict a **state** and treat it grammatically as an **action done by the thing itself**.
Verbs that look like English "is" or a passive

本が分かる is usually rendered "I understand the book". But the carriage is **本**. It is the book that does the verb. The nearest English is "the book is understandable (to me)", and the exact structure is "the book does understandable". 日本語ができる is the same: "Japanese does possible (to me)", not "I do Japanese". This also applies to every potential: 本が読める.

rows: to be chipped, to be lacking
to be reflected, to be shown

blocks.text: English can only use "is" or the passive for these, so translators do too. That is fine for telling someone what was said, but not for building your own sentences. If you look for a passive form you will go wrong. Say it as an action by the thing itself.

濡れる, "become wet", is a change. Put it into 〜ている and you get the state it leaves: 濡れている, "is wet", literally "keeps doing wet". 濁っている is "is cloudy". Remember the verb is self-move: nothing else is acting on the thing.

blocks.jp: 傘がないので、服が濡れた。
blocks.en: Without an umbrella, my clothes got wet.
The moon is reflected in the window.

blocks.jp: この川は少し濁っている。
blocks.en: This river is a little cloudy.

blocks.jp: 私は英語が少しできる。
blocks.en: I can do a little English. (English does possible to me)

items: Japanese has **no passive voice**; many verbs just describe a state as an action of the thing itself.
**本が分かる / 日本語ができる**: the が noun is the carriage.
**乱れる, 欠ける, 映る, 濡れる, 濁る** are self-move verbs of state or change.
**〜ている** turns a change into the state that follows.

questions.instruction: In 本が分かる, which noun is the carriage?
questions.note: が marks the carriage: the book does understandable.

questions.prompt: Japanese verbs like 乱れる are passives.
questions.note: They are active verbs of state or change done by the thing itself.

questions.instruction: Which is the state of being wet?
questions.note: 濡れる + ている: keeps being wet.

questions.instruction: Which verb is the natural way to say "the moon is reflected"?
questions.note: 映る is a self-move verb of state.

questions.instruction: What kind of verb is 濁る?
questions.note: Cloudiness is something the water itself does.

questions.instruction: Why do translators use "is" or the passive for these verbs?
options: English has no natural active form for them
questions.note: That is a translation need, not Japanese structure.

questions.instruction: Which sentence has the thing as its own doer?
Which pair is the "Adam and Eve" of Japanese verbs?
options: あげる and くれる

questions.prompt: My clothes got wet in the rain.

questions.instruction: What does 川が濁っている say?
questions.note: The state that results from becoming cloudy.
